questions.question: During the takeoff roll, how should a pilot determine the degree of control attained and manage the flight controls?
questions.correct_answer: By sensing the control resistance to pressure and the airplane's reaction, rather than by the movement of the controls.
distractors: By observing the physical movement of the controls, which is the only real indicator of controllability.
By referencing the airplane's airspeed, as control resistance is a direct measure of speed.
By anticipating the airplane's reaction and adjusting control movements before feeling any resistance.
questions.explanation: According to the AFH, the feel of resistance to the movement of the controls and the airplane's reaction are the only real indicators of the degree of control attained. This resistance indicates controllability, not speed. Therefore, the pilot should wait for the airplane's reaction to applied control pressures and attempt to sense this resistance, rather than trying to control the airplane simply by the physical movement of the controls.

reference.text:
The feel of resistance to the movement of the controls and the airplane’s reaction to such movements are the only real indicators of
the degree of control attained. This feel of resistance is not a measure of the airplane’s speed, but rather of its controllability. To
determine the degree of controllability, the pilot should be conscious of the reaction of the airplane to the control pressures and
immediately adjust the pressures as needed to control the airplane. The pilot should wait for the reaction of the airplane to the applied
control pressures and attempt to sense the control resistance to pressure rather than attempt to control the airplane by movement of the
controls.

questions.question: During the initial climb immediately after liftoff, what is the likely consequence if a pilot relaxes back-elevator pressure before the proper climb speed is established?
questions.correct_answer: The airplane may settle back toward the ground and potentially contact the runway.
distractors: The airplane will experience an accelerated stall due to a sudden loss of airspeed.
The airplane will pitch up aggressively due to the takeoff trim setting, requiring immediate forward pressure.
The airplane will rapidly accelerate beyond Vy (best rate of climb speed) and require a reduction in power.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook (AFH) Chapter 6, during the initial climb, some back-elevator pressure may be required to hold the climb attitude until the proper climb speed is established. If a pilot relaxes this back-elevator pressure prematurely, the aircraft's angle of attack decreases, resulting in a loss of lift. This can cause the airplane to settle, potentially to the extent that it contacts the runway.

reference.text:
If the airplane has been properly trimmed for takeoff, some back-elevator pressure may be required to hold this attitude until the
proper climb speed is established. Relaxation of any back-elevator pressure before this time may result in the airplane settling, even to
the extent that it contacts the runway.

questions.question: During initial climb, what is the disadvantage of maintaining VY compared to using a lower pitch for cruise climb in the event of a powerplant failure?
questions.correct_answer: The higher pitch attitude at VY leaves less airspeed margin above stall speed, requiring much quicker pilot response to preclude a stall.
distractors: VY causes the engine to run hotter, increasing the likelihood of a powerplant failure during climb.
VY results in a steeper descent angle after engine failure, making it harder to reach a suitable landing area.
VY reduces rudder authority, making it more difficult to maintain directional control after a powerplant failure.
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 6, the pilot should consider flying at a lower pitch for cruise climb since flying at VY requires much quicker pilot response in the event of a powerplant failure to preclude a stall. At VY, the higher pitch attitude means the aircraft is closer to stall speed, so when power is lost, the airspeed decelerates toward stall more rapidly, leaving the pilot less time to lower the nose. The distractors are incorrect because the power setting is the same in both cases (takeoff power), the concern is stall prevention—not glide angle or rudder authority—and the handbook specifically identifies stall avoidance as the safety issue.

reference.text:
The airplane’s speed will increase rapidly after it becomes airborne. Once a positive rate of climb is established, the pilot should
retract the flaps and landing gear (if equipped). It is recommended that takeoff power be maintained until reaching an altitude of at
least 500 feet above the surrounding terrain or obstacles. The combination of VY and takeoff power assures the maximum altitude
gained in a minimum amount of time. This gives the pilot more altitude from which the airplane can be safely maneuvered in case of
an engine failure or other emergency. The pilot should also consider flying at a lower pitch for cruise climb since flying at VY
requires much quicker pilot response in the event of a powerplant failure to preclude a stall.

questions.question: During a student pilot's first solo flight, the airplane lifts off earlier and climbs more rapidly than expected. According to the AFH, what is the primary risk this poses to the subsequent landing?
questions.correct_answer: The anxiety caused by the unexpected takeoff performance can persist and result in poor landing performance
distractors: The lighter aircraft requires a significantly lower approach speed, which the student may not apply
The flight controls will feel less sensitive during landing due to the decreased weight
The student must use a lower pitch attitude on landing to compensate for the lighter aircraft
questions.explanation: The AFH states that when a student pilot is surprised by the improved takeoff performance on their first solo (earlier liftoff and more rapid climb due to decreased weight), the resulting anxiety and uncertainty from perceiving an 'abnormal' takeoff can persist until after the landing, frequently resulting in poor landing performance. The issue is psychological, not a required change in landing technique. The distractors are incorrect because the handbook does not identify a need to change approach speed or landing pitch attitude for the solo flight, and the controls would feel MORE sensitive, not less, due to decreased weight.

reference.text:
When the student pilot nears the solo stage of flight training, it should be explained that the airplane’s takeoff performance will be
much different when the instructor is not in the airplane. Due to decreased load, the airplane will become airborne earlier and climb
more rapidly. The pitch attitude that the student has learned to associate with initial climb may also differ due to decreased weight,
and the flight controls may seem more sensitive. If the situation is unexpected, it may result in increased anxiety that may remain until
after the landing. Frequently, the existence of this anxiety and the uncertainty that develops due to the perception of an “abnormal”
takeoff results in poor performance on the subsequent landing.

questions.question: During a takeoff roll in a crosswind from the right, what effect does the left-yawing tendency from P-factor have on the airplane's weathervaning tendency?
questions.correct_answer: It may counteract the airplane's tendency to weathervane into the wind.
distractors: It may aggravate the airplane's tendency to weathervane into the wind.
It eliminates the need for the pilot to apply rudder pressure during the takeoff roll.
It causes the airplane to weathervane to the left rather than into the wind.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, during a takeoff roll in a crosswind from the right, the airplane tends to weathervane to the right. The resulting P-factor causes the airplane to yaw to the left, which may counteract this weathervaning tendency. Conversely, in a crosswind from the left, P-factor would aggravate the weathervaning tendency. In any case, the pilot must use appropriate rudder pressure to keep the airplane rolling straight down the runway.

reference.text:
While holding aileron pressure into the wind, the pilot should use the rudder to maintain a straight takeoff path. [Figure 6-4] Since
the airplane tends to weathervane into the wind while on the ground, the pilot will typically apply downwind rudder pressure. When
the pilot increases power for takeoff, the resulting P-factor causes the airplane to yaw to the left. While this yaw may be sufficient to
counteract the airplane’s tendency to weathervane into the wind in a crosswind from the right, it may aggravate this tendency in a
crosswind from the left. In any case, the pilot should apply rudder pressure in the appropriate direction to keep the airplane rolling
straight down the runway.

questions.question: When an airplane leaves ground effect during takeoff, it experiences a pitch-up tendency. What is the primary cause of this pitching moment?
questions.correct_answer: An increase in downwash at the horizontal tail
distractors: A decrease in downwash at the horizontal tail
An increase in induced drag on the main wings
A reduction in static source pressure
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 6, when an airplane leaves ground effect during takeoff, it experiences a pitch-up tendency due to an increase in downwash at the horizontal tail. The increased downwash creates a greater downward force on the tail surface, causing the nose to pitch up. Note that while an increase in induced drag and a reduction in static source pressure are also effects of leaving ground effect, they are not the cause of the pitch-up tendency. A decrease in downwash would produce the opposite effect.

reference.text:
⦁ The airplane requires an increase in AOA to maintain lift coefficient.
    ⦁ The airplane experiences an increase in induced drag and thrust required.
    ⦁ The airplane experiences a pitch-up tendency and requires less elevator travel because of an increase
      in downwash at the horizontal tail.
    ⦁ The airplane experiences a reduction in static source pressure and a corresponding increase in
      indicated airspeed.

questions.question: During takeoff, a pilot observes a sudden increase in indicated airspeed as the aircraft climbs out of ground effect. What aerodynamic phenomenon explains this indication change?
questions.correct_answer: Static source pressure decreases upon leaving ground effect, causing the airspeed indicator to display a higher indicated airspeed.
distractors: Ram air pressure at the pitot tube increases as the aircraft accelerates out of ground effect, causing the higher indication.
Static source pressure increases upon leaving ground effect, resulting in a larger differential pressure and higher indicated airspeed.
Induced drag decreases out of ground effect, allowing a true airspeed increase that is immediately reflected on the airspeed indicator.
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 6, leaving ground effect during takeoff causes a reduction in static source pressure and a corresponding increase in indicated airspeed. The airspeed indicator measures the difference between pitot (total) pressure and static pressure. When static pressure drops at the static port while total pressure remains essentially unchanged, the differential increases and the indicator reads higher. This is an instrument indication effect, not an actual acceleration of the aircraft. Distractor 1 incorrectly attributes the change to pitot ram pressure. Distractor 2 reverses the static pressure change direction. Distractor 3 incorrectly states induced drag decreases out of ground effect — it actually increases — and conflates true airspeed with the indication change.

reference.text:
⦁ The airplane requires an increase in AOA to maintain lift coefficient.
    ⦁ The airplane experiences an increase in induced drag and thrust required.
    ⦁ The airplane experiences a pitch-up tendency and requires less elevator travel because of an increase
      in downwash at the horizontal tail.
    ⦁ The airplane experiences a reduction in static source pressure and a corresponding increase in
      indicated airspeed.

questions.question: An airplane lifts off below recommended airspeed and is unable to climb out of ground effect due to high density altitude and maximum gross weight. Since the initial takeoff and climb is already based on maximum power, what must the pilot do to resolve this situation?
questions.correct_answer: Reduce drag by reducing pitch, even if it means losing altitude
distractors: Increase pitch to generate the additional lift needed to climb out of ground effect
Apply full power to overcome the increased drag encountered outside ground effect
Maintain the current pitch attitude and accelerate in ground effect until climb is possible
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 6, when an airplane cannot climb out of ground effect, reducing drag is the only option because the initial takeoff and climb is already based on maximum power—no additional power is available. To reduce drag, the pilot must reduce pitch, which means losing altitude. Increasing pitch would increase drag and worsen the situation. Applying full power is not an option because power is already at maximum. Simply maintaining pitch and accelerating in ground effect does not address the fundamental drag problem and may still result in the inability to clear obstructions.

reference.text:
Due to the reduced drag in ground effect, the airplane may seem to be able to take off below the recommended airspeed. However, as
the airplane climbs out of ground effect below the recommended climb speed, initial climb performance will be much less than at VY
or even VX. Under conditions of high density altitude, high temperature, and/or maximum gross weight, the airplane may be able to
lift off but will be unable to climb out of ground effect. Consequently, the airplane may not be able to clear obstructions. Lift-off
before attaining recommended flight airspeed incurs more drag, which requires more power to overcome. Since the initial takeoff and
climb is based on maximum power, reducing drag is the only option. To reduce drag, pitch should be reduced which means losing
altitude. Pilots should remember that many airplanes cannot safely takeoff at maximum gross weight at certain altitudes and
temperatures, due to lack of performance. Therefore, under marginal conditions, it is important that the airplane takes off at the speed
recommended for adequate initial climb performance.

questions.question: During takeoff at high density altitude and maximum gross weight, the airplane lifts off but is unable to climb out of ground effect. With the engine already producing maximum power, what should the pilot do to address the excessive drag?
questions.correct_answer: Reduce pitch to decrease drag, accepting a temporary loss of altitude
distractors: Increase pitch to generate additional lift and climb away from the ground
Maintain the current pitch attitude and wait for the airplane to accelerate
Retract the flaps to reduce drag while holding the current pitch attitude
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 6, when an airplane lifts off below recommended airspeed, it incurs more drag that requires more power to overcome. Since the engine is already at maximum power, reducing drag is the only option. The handbook states: 'To reduce drag, pitch should be reduced which means losing altitude.' Increasing pitch would add more induced drag, worsening the situation. Waiting for acceleration is not viable because the airplane is already at maximum power with no excess thrust available. Retracting flaps is not the recommended corrective action and could cause a dangerous loss of lift near the ground.

reference.text:
Due to the reduced drag in ground effect, the airplane may seem to be able to take off below the recommended airspeed. However, as
the airplane climbs out of ground effect below the recommended climb speed, initial climb performance will be much less than at VY
or even VX. Under conditions of high density altitude, high temperature, and/or maximum gross weight, the airplane may be able to
lift off but will be unable to climb out of ground effect. Consequently, the airplane may not be able to clear obstructions. Lift-off
before attaining recommended flight airspeed incurs more drag, which requires more power to overcome. Since the initial takeoff and
climb is based on maximum power, reducing drag is the only option. To reduce drag, pitch should be reduced which means losing
altitude. Pilots should remember that many airplanes cannot safely takeoff at maximum gross weight at certain altitudes and
temperatures, due to lack of performance. Therefore, under marginal conditions, it is important that the airplane takes off at the speed
recommended for adequate initial climb performance.

questions.question: When taking off from an unsatisfactory surface, which technique should the pilot employ during the ground run and lift-off?
questions.correct_answer: Apply as much weight to the wings as possible, using ground effect as an aid prior to attaining true flying speed
distractors: Maintain weight on the wheels until reaching rotation speed to ensure adequate directional control
Delay lift-off until the aircraft reaches a speed well above normal rotation speed
Increase the angle of attack to climb out of ground effect as quickly as possible
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 6, when taking off from an unsatisfactory surface, the pilot should apply as much weight to the wings as possible during the ground run and lift-off, using ground effect as an aid prior to attaining true flying speed. This reduces the load on the landing gear while the aircraft is on the rough surface. The pilot should then reduce AOA to attain normal airspeed before attempting to fly out of the ground effect area. Maintaining weight on the wheels delays the benefit of unloading the gear. Waiting for a speed well above rotation speed ignores the advantage ground effect provides. Increasing AOA to climb out prematurely risks dragging the tail and does not follow the recommended procedure of first reducing AOA to gain airspeed before leaving ground effect.

reference.text:
When taking off from an unsatisfactory surface, the pilot should apply as much weight to the wings as possible during the ground run
and lift-off, using ground effect as an aid, prior to attaining true flying speed. The pilot should reduce AOA to attain normal airspeed
before attempting to fly out of the ground effect areas.

questions.question: During takeoff, if the airplane becomes airborne before reaching VX, what characteristic of the initial climb creates a concern for obstacle clearance?
questions.correct_answer: The climb remains flat, diminishing the pilot's ability to successfully perform the climb and/or clear obstacles.
distractors: The airplane accelerates too slowly after lift-off, requiring the pilot to lower the nose to regain airspeed.
The climb becomes excessively steep, increasing the risk of the airplane settling back to the runway.
The airplane requires continuous forward elevator pressure to prevent an accelerated stall.
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 6, even if the airplane remains airborne, until the pilot reaches VX the initial climb will remain flat, which diminishes the pilot's ability to successfully perform the climb and/or clear obstacles. The handbook notes that the airplane actually accelerates more rapidly after lift-off, making the first distractor incorrect. The second distractor describes the opposite of what occurs—a flat climb, not a steep one. The third distractor is unsupported; the handbook advises applying additional back-elevator pressure to hold a constant airspeed, not forward pressure.

reference.text:
Lift-Off
As VX approaches, the pilot should apply back-elevator pressure until reaching the appropriate VX attitude to ensure a smooth and
firm lift-off, or rotation. Since the airplane accelerates more rapidly after lift-off, the pilot should apply additional back-
elevator pressure to hold a constant airspeed. After becoming airborne, the pilot will maintain a wings-level climb at VX until all
obstacles have been cleared, or if no obstacles are present, until reaching an altitude of at least 50 feet above the takeoff surface.
Thereafter, the pilot may lower the pitch attitude slightly and continue the climb at VY until reaching a safe maneuvering altitude. The
pilot should always remember that an attempt to pull the airplane off the ground prematurely, or to climb too steeply, may cause
the airplane to settle back to the runway or make contact with obstacles. Even if the airplane remains airborne, until the pilot reaches
VX, the initial climb will remain flat, which diminishes the pilot's ability to successfully perform the climb and/or clear obstacles.
[Figure 6-9]

questions.question: If a pilot maintains a nose-high attitude throughout the takeoff roll, the airplane may lift off at an airspeed slower than a safe climb speed. What primarily allows the airplane to become airborne at this reduced airspeed?
questions.correct_answer: Ground effect reduces induced drag, permitting flight at an airspeed that would otherwise be too slow for safe climbing flight.
distractors: Propeller slipstream flowing over the wings at the high pitch angle provides additional lift at low airspeeds.
Reduced weight on the wheels minimizes rolling friction, allowing the airplane to reach liftoff speed more quickly than normal.
The high angle of attack alone generates sufficient lift to sustain flight regardless of airspeed.
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 6, when a nose-high attitude is accurately maintained throughout the takeoff run, the airplane 'virtually flies itself off the ground' due to ground effect, becoming airborne at an airspeed slower than a safe climb speed. Ground effect is the key factor—it reduces induced drag near the surface, allowing the wings to produce enough lift for flight at an otherwise inadequate airspeed. The distractors are wrong because: (1) propeller slipstream is not the cause described in the handbook; (2) reduced rolling friction explains faster acceleration but not lifting off at a slower-than-safe speed; and (3) the high angle of attack alone would not sustain flight at such low airspeed without ground effect.

reference.text:
When the airplane is held at a nose-high attitude throughout the takeoff run, the wings increasingly relieve the wheels of the airplane’s
weight as speed increases and lift develops, thereby minimizing the drag caused by surface irregularities or adhesion. If this attitude is
accurately maintained, the airplane virtually flies itself off the ground, becoming airborne but at an airspeed slower than a safe climb
speed because of ground effect. [Figure 6-10]

questions.question: During the takeoff roll, maintaining a nose-high attitude allows the wings to relieve the wheels of the airplane's weight. What is the result if the airplane virtually "flies itself off" the ground in this manner?
questions.correct_answer: It becomes airborne at an airspeed slower than a safe climb speed due to ground effect.
distractors: It becomes airborne at an airspeed much faster than a safe climb speed due to reduced induced drag.
It remains grounded because ground effect increases the drag caused by surface irregularities.
It requires a higher rotation speed to overcome the increased adhesion of the wheels to the surface.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, holding a nose-high attitude throughout the takeoff run allows the wings to relieve the wheels of weight, minimizing drag from surface irregularities. The airplane may then 'fly itself off' the ground, becoming airborne at an airspeed slower than a safe climb speed because of ground effect.

reference.text:
When the airplane is held at a nose-high attitude throughout the takeoff run, the wings increasingly relieve the wheels of the airplane’s
weight as speed increases and lift develops, thereby minimizing the drag caused by surface irregularities or adhesion. If this attitude is
accurately maintained, the airplane virtually flies itself off the ground, becoming airborne but at an airspeed slower than a safe climb
speed because of ground effect. [Figure 6-10]

questions.question: During initial climb-out, your engine fails and you are tempted to turn back to the departure runway. According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, what determines whether a turn-back maneuver should be attempted?
questions.correct_answer: Only if the pilot has previously trained for an emergency turn-back and sufficient altitude exists
distractors: It should be attempted whenever sufficient altitude exists to complete the turn back to the runway
It should be attempted if the pilot holds at least a private pilot certificate, regardless of altitude
It should never be attempted under any circumstances following an engine failure on climb-out
questions.explanation: The AFH states that attempting to turn back to the takeoff runway should not be attempted unless the pilot has previously trained for an emergency turn-back AND sufficient altitude exists. Both conditions must be met. Distractor 1 ignores the training requirement. Distractor 2 confuses standard certification with specific turn-back training and ignores altitude. Distractor 3 is too absolute—the handbook does allow a turn-back if both conditions are satisfied. The pilot's first priority is maintaining aircraft control by lowering the nose to prevent a stall and establishing a controlled glide, preferably straight ahead.

reference.text:
In the event of an engine failure on initial climb-out, the pilot’s first responsibility is to maintain aircraft control. At a climb pitch
attitude without power, the airplane is at or near a stalling AOA. At the same time, the pilot may still be holding right rudder. The
pilot should immediately lower the nose to prevent a stall while moving the rudder to ensure coordinated flight. The pilot should
establish a controlled glide toward a plausible landing area, preferably straight ahead. Attempting to turn back to the takeoff runway
should not be attempted unless the pilot previously trained for an emergency turn-back and sufficient altitude exists.

questions.question: The Airplane Flying Handbook notes that the takeoff and departure phase of flight is short but involves intense pilot workload, resulting in about 20 percent of all general aviation accidents. What specifically causes a significant number of these takeoff accidents?
questions.correct_answer: Loss of control of the airplane
distractors: Loss of engine power during the climb
Loss of situational awareness in the traffic pattern
Loss of visual reference with the runway environment
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook (AFH) Chapter 6, while about twenty percent of all yearly GA accidents occur during takeoff and departure climbs, a significant number of these specific takeoff accidents are the direct result of a loss of control of the airplane by the pilot.

reference.text:
Introduction
About twenty percent of all yearly general aviation (GA) accidents occur during takeoff and departure climbs, and more than half of
those accidents are the result of some sort of failure of the pilot. A significant number of takeoff accidents are the result of loss of
control of the airplane. When compared to the entire profile of a normal flight, this phase of a flight is relatively short, but the pilot
workload is intense. This chapter discusses takeoffs and departure climbs in airplanes under normal conditions and under conditions
that require maximum performance.

questions.question: Despite being a relatively short part of a normal flight, the takeoff and departure climb phase accounts for roughly twenty percent of yearly general aviation accidents. According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, what primary characteristic makes this phase particularly challenging?
distractors: The pilot workload is minimal, which often leads to complacency.
The aircraft is typically operated at its maximum ceiling altitude.
The phase requires continuous communication with air traffic control.
questions.explanation: The Airplane Flying Handbook states that when compared to the entire profile of a normal flight, the takeoff and departure climb phase is relatively short, but the pilot workload is intense. This high workload contributes to the fact that a significant percentage of general aviation accidents occur during this phase.

reference.text:
Introduction
About twenty percent of all yearly general aviation (GA) accidents occur during takeoff and departure climbs, and more than half of
those accidents are the result of some sort of failure of the pilot. A significant number of takeoff accidents are the result of loss of
control of the airplane. When compared to the entire profile of a normal flight, this phase of a flight is relatively short, but the pilot
workload is intense. This chapter discusses takeoffs and departure climbs in airplanes under normal conditions and under conditions
that require maximum performance.

questions.question: While reviewing takeoff procedures, a pilot finds that the flap configuration recommended in the Airplane Flying Handbook (AFH) differs from the configuration listed in the airplane's Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH). Which source should the pilot use?
questions.correct_answer: The POH, because the airplane manufacturer's recommendations take precedence over the AFH.
distractors: The AFH, because it is an FAA-approved document and provides generalized procedures for all aircraft.
The procedure that yields the shortest takeoff roll, regardless of which manual it comes from.
The AFH, because the POH only takes precedence for operating limitations, not for normal takeoff procedures.
questions.explanation: According to Chapter 6 of the Airplane Flying Handbook, if any information in the handbook differs from the airplane manufacturer's recommendations as contained in the FAA-approved AFM/POH, the airplane manufacturer's recommendations take precedence. This applies to airplane configuration, airspeeds, and other information relevant to takeoffs and departure climbs.

reference.text:
The discussion in this chapter is centered on airplanes with tricycle landing gear (nose-wheel). Procedures for conventional gear
airplanes (tail-wheel) are discussed in Chapter 14: Transition to Tailwheel Airplanes. The manufacturer’s recommended procedures
pertaining to airplane configuration, airspeeds, and other information relevant to takeoffs and departure climbs in a specific make and
model airplane are contained in the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)-approved Airplane Flight Manual and/or Pilot’s
Operating Handbook (AFM/POH) for that airplane. If any of the information in this chapter differs from the airplane manufacturer’s
recommendations as contained in the AFM/POH, the airplane manufacturer’s recommendations take precedence.

questions.question: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, when is the initial climb considered complete?
questions.correct_answer: When the airplane has reached a safe maneuvering altitude or an en route climb has been established.
distractors: When the airplane leaves the surface and a climb pitch attitude has been established.
When the airplane reaches pattern altitude and levels off for the downwind leg.
When the landing gear and flaps have been fully retracted.
questions.explanation: The Airplane Flying Handbook states that the initial climb begins when the airplane leaves the surface and a climb pitch attitude has been established. It is considered complete when the airplane has reached a safe maneuvering altitude or an en route climb has been established. Leaving the surface marks the beginning of the climb, not the completion.

reference.text:
⦁ The initial climb begins when the airplane leaves the surface and a climb pitch attitude has been established.
      Normally, it is considered complete when the airplane has reached a safe maneuvering altitude or an en
      route climb has been established.
